what: The HTML Entity Encoder and Decoder converts characters into HTML entities, such as < for < and é for é, and turns entities back into normal text.

Decoding uses the full list of 2,125 HTML5 entity names plus decimal and hex numbers, following the same rules as browsers, including old names without a semicolon and the special meaning of numbers 128 to 159.
uses: Showing code on a web page
Encode < and > so HTML or XML examples display instead of running.
Escape user text before putting it into HTML attributes or content.
Decode &, " and ' in text copied from page sources or APIs.
Encode every non-ASCII character for systems that do not handle UTF-8 well.
tutorial: Paste plain text to encode or HTML with entities to decode.
Only < > & " ' is enough for UTF-8 pages; add every non-ASCII character or every character if needed.
Names where possible (é), decimal (é) or hex (é).

Encode quotes, show non-breaking spaces as  , or turn line breaks into
.
Press Encode or Decode. The message tells you how many entities were converted and lists unknown names.
Copy the result, or press Use result as input to process it again.
features: Numbers 128–159 map to Windows-1252 characters, invalid numbers become �, and legacy names work without a semicolon.
HTML-special only, all non-ASCII, or every character.
Characters outside the basic plane are encoded as one number, like 😀.
Megabytes of text in about a second, in your browser.

example.title: Showing HTML code in a blog post
example.text: Paste Home and press Encode. The result <a href="/">Home</a> displays as code on your page instead of becoming a link.

tips: For UTF-8 pages, encode only the special characters; there is no need to encode accented letters.
Inside attribute values, always encode quotes.
Decode twice if you see &amp;: the text was encoded twice.
Use hex numbers when matching code points from a character map.
problems: The name is misspelled or not an HTML entity. Check the spelling, including upper and lower case: É and é differ.
A dash appeared instead of a number
Numbers 128 to 159 stand for Windows-1252 characters in HTML; – is –. This matches how browsers read them.
Browsers read &copy without a semicolon as ©. Write &copyright if you mean the literal text.
